properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL (Anthony, 2026-10-12, thinking out loud; nothing here is chosen).

THE FRAME, his words: "I feel like the decision/design process that we've put in place follows: The main concept of Nassim Nicholas Taleb's book Antifragile: Things That Gain from Disorder is that certain systems, bodies, and ideas actually benefit and grow stronger when exposed to volatility, randomness, stress, and disorder." He listed Taleb's core concepts:
- the fragile / robust / antifragile trichotomy;
- the barbell strategy;
- via negativa ("improving a system by subtracting harmful, fragile elements or unnecessary interventions rather than adding complex rules, top-down control, or bureaucratic fixes");
- skin in the game;
- the Lindy effect;
- tinkering over academic theory.

"I feel that reflow2 fits the definition of "antifragile" well in that with every interaction with it, it becomes stronger and stronger. It is why I almost don't fear that I can mess it up by making some decision. I think this also applies with anybody else that uses reflow2/flo2.io in their design. The more scrutiny and decision and trials the design goes through, I feel that the design becomes "antifragile". That's mostly just an observation. I think "Bottom-up practical experimentation, trial and error, and heuristic learning almost always outperform top-down theoretical models or academic planning" is also along these lines."

THE QUESTION, his words: "What I'd like to brainstorm is introducing "via negativa" as maybe a skill or even an enduring principle if reflow2 that every decision it makes, it uses via negativa as a design principle".

WHERE reflow2 ALREADY MATCHES HIS FRAME (observations, not claims of proof):
- Skin in the game: a decision only counts with a person's name on it (rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word).
- Tinkering: reflow2 and flo2 are exercised by repeated three-agent design trials (rule:reflow2-and-flo2-are-exercised-by-a-three-agent-design-trial).
- Not fearing a mistake: every replaced value is kept in a snapshot, roads not taken are kept, and a settled decision can be reopened. A wrong move is cheap to undo, which is the asymmetry Taleb praises.

OPTIONS, none chosen:
(a) An enduring principle, advisory like rule:reflow2-is-one-of-three-parts-and-does-not-compete-with-the-others: before adding anything (a requirement, capability, rule, tool, step, field), ask what could be taken away instead.
(b) A step in the skills where decisions are made (brainstorm, capture-intent, revise-design, root-cause step ⑧, optimize): name what this lets you remove, or why nothing can be.
(c) A skill of its own that walks a design for things to remove: requirements nobody satisfies or needs, duplicated rules, decisions superseded but not retired, capabilities nothing realizes, tools nobody calls.
(d) Make it measurable: the design reports what was taken away beside what was added over time, so a design that only ever grows is visible.
(e) Apply it to reflow2 itself first, through the open dec:idea-reflow2-does-fewer-things-and-does-them-really-well and dec:idea-prune-the-tool-surface-to-an-orthogonal-essential-set.
properties.name: SETTLED 2026-10-12 — via negativa kept as an ADVISORY question, barbell-style: before a structural addition, ask what could be taken away; never take away from the record. Measuring removals beside additions comes later
properties.rationale:
Counter-arguments and costs, recorded beside the idea, not against it:

1. A RULE THAT EVERY DECISION MUST SUBTRACT IS ITSELF AN ADDED TOP-DOWN RULE, the thing via negativa warns against. An advisory lens (a question asked, not a gate that fails a build) avoids the irony; (a) as a gate would not.

2. SUBTRACT FROM THE LIVING SYSTEM, NEVER FROM THE RECORD. The safety he describes ("I almost don't fear that I can mess it up") comes from reflow2 keeping everything: prior values, roads not taken, history. That kept record is the optionality that makes trying things cheap. Applied to the record, via negativa would destroy exactly what makes the design antifragile. Any version needs that line: take away what is built, required or ruled, keep what is remembered.

3. LINDY SAYS WHAT TO REMOVE FIRST. Taleb's own pairing: the newest, least-tested additions are the most fragile, and what has survived longest is likeliest to keep surviving. reflow2 adds a lot from single measured failures (lessons carried on tool descriptions, paragraphs in skills, new rules). Each was added for a measured reason (rule:a-lesson-is-generalised-before-it-is-built), so taking one away needs evidence too: that it stopped earning its place.

4. THE ANTIFRAGILE CLAIM HOLDS WHERE STRESS REACHES THE RECORD, AND NOT AUTOMATICALLY. Measured 2026-10-12 by loop_status on reflow2's design: real runs have been compared against 78 of 440 checks, most recently on 2026-09-23, and none has ever fed back a failure. Failures reach the design today through findings and root causes written by hand. That happened four times in this one session, each making the design stronger. Every interaction makes it stronger when someone records what went wrong; the checks themselves do not yet learn from failing runs.

5. COST PER DECISION, which argues for a barbell: asking "what can we remove?" on every small decision is noise. Ask it hard on structural decisions (a new requirement, capability, tool, rule or skill) and lightly or not at all on small ones.

6. COSTS, roughly:
- (a) is one node and a sentence in the served instructions. Cheapest.
- (b) is text in five skills, which also makes every skill longer: the irony again.
- (c) is a new skill, moderate; much of it could reuse existing detectors (orphans, duplicates, unrealized and superseded nodes).
- (d) needs code and a release, the larger cost, but it is the only option that makes the principle checkable rather than hoped for.
- (e) is the largest, with its own open questions.
